Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

issues.explanation: For a witnessed-other-trauma profile, 'being seen' and 'being criticised or corrected' are hard to reconcile as primary trauma triggers unless the witnessed event specifically involved scrutiny or humiliation; nothing else in the profile supports that context.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected
issues.explanation: The formulation has a strong Triggers → Threat link, so trigger content should plausibly map onto the endorsed threat meanings. 'Time of day the event occurred' links well with hypervigilance to sounds, but 'being seen' and 'being criticised' do not connect clearly to the selected threat items.

vignette:
Karim, a 41-year-old Middle Eastern man who worked the evening shift at a fast food restaurant, described his symptoms as beginning after a night when he was leaving work and witnessed a violent altercation in the parking lot. It had been around the same hour he now dreaded, just after the dinner rush had quieted and the lobby lights were being dimmed, when a sudden series of loud bangs-first from a car backfiring, then from one of the men slamming a door-made him turn toward the lot. In the confusion he saw someone on the ground and another person shouting, and for a few seconds he felt frozen in place, aware only of the noise, the harsh sounds of voices, and the sense that something terrible was unfolding without warning. Since then, certain moments have carried that night back into him with an almost physical force. If a supervisor corrected him sharply at work, even about something small like the way a tray was stocked, he would feel his body brace and his mind jump immediately to danger, as if criticism meant trouble was already building around him. He noticed the same reaction when the clock moved toward that same time of evening, because that was when the event had happened and when his shift still felt most exposed to him. Loud noises had become especially difficult: a dropped metal pan, a car horn outside the restaurant, or an unexpected shout from the kitchen would snap his attention outward and make him scan for what was about to go wrong.

As those triggers accumulated, Karim came to believe that safety existed only in a very limited number of places, and that outside of them he had to stay constantly on guard. The restaurant, which had once felt routine, began to feel unpredictable; the parking lot after closing was unbearable, and even in the dining room he watched the doors and listened for abrupt sounds. He was on high alert when he heard anything unexpected or loud, and when something took longer than expected he assumed something bad was happening. If a coworker was late returning from break, or a customer stayed too long outside by the window, his thoughts quickly turned to threat, as though delay itself meant an emergency was developing just out of sight. This way of reading the world narrowed his life further. He stopped lingering after shifts, took longer routes home that felt more controlled, and avoided being alone in unfamiliar places. He could still function, but only by arranging his days around the few places that felt tolerable, and that shrinking of his world left him more isolated.

Over the following months, the pattern strengthened. Because he expected danger to announce itself through criticism, delays, and sudden sound, he found himself watching and listening with exhausting intensity, always braced for the next sign that something bad was about to happen. At work he became tense when a manager raised a voice across the counter, even if the correction was ordinary, and he would spend the rest of the shift scanning for the source of every clang, shout, or pause in the flow of customers. He said that the waiting was often worse than the event itself: if an order was running behind or a car sat idling too long outside, his mind filled in the worst possibility before anyone had even explained what was happening. That sense of being boxed in by threat made it harder for him to trust any setting outside the handful of places he had decided were safe, and the smaller that safe zone became, the more he felt his life organized around avoiding the next shock.

Karim sought help after his manager commented that he had become "too jumpy" and "too tense" during shifts, especially when the kitchen got noisy at closing time. He was embarrassed by how easily criticism set off his alarm, and he was tired of living as if every unexpected sound or delay meant something terrible was unfolding. What brought him in was not only the strain at work but the fear that his world had become permanently narrowed, with safety available only in a few carefully chosen places. He hoped therapy might help him stop assuming the worst every time a noise broke the silence or a minute ran long, but he was most afraid that he would never feel settled enough to move through an ordinary day without scanning for danger.
